rows.question: An internal portal renders successfully for some users and fails for others. The bug affects only one browser family and only on desktop. Local testing is clean. Diagnose the likely cause and propose a minimal diagnostic sequence.
rows.answer:
Medical safety note: this is general information, not a diagnosis or a substitute for a licensed clinician.

To diagnose this issue, I'd suggest the following steps: 1. Browser and OS Specific Testing: Try accessing the portal exclusively in the affected browser (e.g., Chrome) on both Windows and macOS desktop operating systems to check if it's an OS-specific bug. 2. Network Connectivity Check: Test network connectivity between your local machine and the server hosting the portal by running a simple speed test and checking for any latency issues during the access attempt. This can help rule out network-related problems. 3. Browser Extensions and Plugins: Disable all browser extensions (including ad-blockers) and plugins to see if they're causing the issue. Re-enable them one by one to check which extension or plugin is problematic. 4. Clear Browser Cache and Cookies: Clear your browser's cache, cookies, and local storage, then attempt to access the portal again. If it works after clearing these data, you might be dealing with cached resources. 5. Check for CSS Issues: Inspect the HTML and CSS code of the affected pages in the browser's tools. Look for any CSS errors or issues that might be causing layout problems. 6. Use Browser's Tools Network Tab: Access the portal page using browser's tools (F12 keys) and check the network tab while loading the page to see if there are any slow-loading resources causing the issue. 7. Check For Server Errors or Response Codes: Look at the server console logs for any error messages or response codes returned from the server when the request is made. This can give a clue as to what might be wrong. 8. User Agent Spoofing: Try accessing the portal using a different user agent (or spoofed header) in your browser to see if the issue is resolved. 9. Consider Browser Version and Updates: Check for updates on both the browser itself and its extensions/plugins, and install them if necessary. Keep gathering data from these steps and double-check each result before moving on to the next step. It might take some time to narrow down the exact cause of the problem, but following this sequence should help you identify it.

To diagnose this issue, I'd recommend the following steps: 1. Check the user agent string: Since the bug only affects users using a specific browser family on desktop, it's possible that the browser might be playing a role in this problem. Look into the user agent headers for both affected and unaffected users. This will help determine if there are any differences between their browsers. 2. Inspect browser caching: - For affected users, check if they have enabled any cache clearing extensions or manually cleared their browser's cache and cookies before testing. - Compare cached resources like JavaScript files, CSS stylesheets, and images between the affected and unaffected users' profiles. Look for differences in file versions or timestamps. 3. Review network requests: - For both groups, log the network requests made by your application while loading the internal portal. - Examine the request URLs and payloads for any differences. This might reveal discrepancies in how resources are being loaded between affected and unaffected users. 4. Analyze browser compatibility: - Test the internal portal with older versions of the targeted browser family to see if the bug appears there as well. - If the issue is resolved in older versions, it could indicate a recent browser update causing the problem. 5. Consider server-side differences: - Look into any changes made to your server-side code or infrastructure recently that might have introduced this behavior. - Compare configurations and resources between affected and unaffected environments to identify any inconsistencies. 6. Check for JavaScript errors: - For both groups, enable JavaScript errors in their browsers and see if there are any errors reported during the portal loading process. With these steps in mind, you should be able to narrow down the root cause of the issue and find a way to resolve it.

rows.question: A page is broken for only one browser family and only on desktop. The same page works locally for most people. Diagnose the likely cause and propose a minimal investigation plan.
rows.answer: To diagnose this issue with the internal portal that renders successfully for some users but not for others, I'd recommend the following minimal investigation plan: 1. Browser and OS Specific Testing: Try accessing the portal exclusively in the affected browser family on your desktop machine. If you don't have access to a different operating system, try using an emulator to simulate another OS. 2. User Agent String Check: The bug only affects users using a specific browser family. To find out why, check the user agent string sent by that browser when it accesses the page. Look for differences in the headers or request parameters between affected and unaffected browsers. 3. Local Testing of Specific Components: Isolate the components that fail on the problematic desktop browsers. Test each component locally using a simple script to rule out compatibility issues with your server's code. 4. Production Network Inspection: Inspect the network requests made by the affected browser family while it tries to access the portal in production. Look for differences in headers, scripts loaded, cookies set or sent, etc. between affected and unaffected users. 5. Code Review of the Broken Components: If further investigation indicates that a component is broken, review its code to find any errors or logic issues that could be causing the problem. 6. Monitor User Reports: Keep an eye on new user reports. If they start mentioning specific browsers or operating systems, you'll know whether your investigation is narrowing down the cause of the issue. I'd also recommend running this process in parallel with a bug report posted to the relevant issue tracker. The bug report should contain details about the affected browser family and desktop OS, screenshots of the broken page, and code samples of any components that might be causing problems.
